title: Of constancy
paragraphs: The law of resolution and constancy does not mean that we should not, as far as we can, decline and protect ourselves from the harms and inconveniences that threaten us; nor, consequently, that we ought not to fear lest they take us by surprise. On the contrary, all decent and honest ways of guarding ourselves against harm are not only permitted but commendable, and the business of constancy chiefly is to bravely stand up to, and stoutly endure, those inconveniences that cannot possibly be avoided. So there is no supple bodily motion, no movement in handling arms, however irregular or ungraceful, that we need condemn, if it serves to ward off the blow aimed at us.

Several very warlike nations have used a retreating and flying way of fighting as a singular advantage, and by doing so have made their backs more dangerous to their enemies than their faces. The Turks still keep something of this in their practice of arms. Socrates, in Plato, laughs at Laches, who had defined fortitude as standing firm in the ranks against the enemy. "What!" he says, "would it then be cowardice to overcome them by giving ground?" — urging at the same time the authority of Homer, who praises in Aeneas the science of flight. And when Laches, thinking better of it, admits the practice as it applies to the Scythians and, in general, to all cavalry, Socrates attacks him again with the example of the Lacedaemonian foot — a nation of all others the most stubborn in holding their ground — who, at the battle of Plataea, finding they could not break into the Persian phalanx, decided to scatter and retreat, so that the enemy, supposing they fled, should break up and disunite that great mass of men in pursuit; and by this stratagem they won the victory.

As for the Scythians, it is said that when Darius marched out to subdue them, he sent a herald to reproach their king with always retiring before him and avoiding battle. Idanthyrses — that was the king's name — answered that it was not for fear of him or any man living that he did so, but that it was the way of marching practised by his nation, who had neither tilled fields, nor cities, nor houses to defend, nor anything they need fear the enemy might profit by; but, if he had such a stomach to fight, let him just come to view their ancient burial places, and there he should have his fill.

Nevertheless, against cannon-fire, when a body of men is drawn up in front of a train of artillery — as the demands of war often require — it is unbecoming to leave one's post to avoid the danger, since because of its violence and swiftness we reckon it inevitable; and many a man, by ducking, stepping aside, and other such motions of fear, has been thoroughly laughed at by his companions. And yet, in the campaign the Emperor Charles V made into Provence against us, the Marquis del Guasto, going to reconnoitre the city of Arles and stepping out from behind the cover of a windmill under which he had made his approach, was spotted by the Seigneur de Bonneval and the Seneschal of Agenais, who were walking on the theatre aux arenes. They pointed him out to the Sieur de Villiers, commissary of the artillery, who pointed a culverin so admirably well and aimed it so exactly that, had the marquis not slipped aside when he saw the match put to it, it was reckoned certain the shot would have taken him full in the body. And in the same way, some years earlier, Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino and father of the queen-mother, laying siege to Mondolfo, a place in the territories of the Vicariate in Italy, saw the gunner put the match to a piece pointed straight at him. It was well for him that he ducked, for otherwise the shot, which only grazed the top of his head, would no doubt have hit him full in the chest. To tell the truth, I do not think these evasions are performed out of any judgment, for how can any man living judge of high or low aim on so sudden an occasion? It is much easier to believe that fortune favoured their apprehension, and that it might just as well, on another occasion, lead them to face the danger as to seek to avoid it. For my own part, I confess I cannot help starting when the rattle of a harquebus thunders in my ears suddenly, and in a place where I had not expected it — something I have observed in others too, braver fellows than I.

The Stoics do not claim that the philosopher's soul must be proof against the first visions and fantasies that take him by surprise. They agree that, as a natural reflex, he should tremble at the terrible noise of thunder, or at the sudden clatter of some falling ruin, and even turn pale and shake. And so in other passions, provided his judgment remains sound and entire, and that the seat of his reason suffers no shake or alteration, and that he gives no consent to his fright and disturbance. For a man who is not a philosopher, the fright is the same thing in its first phase, but quite another in its second; for the impression of passions does not stay on the surface in him but reaches further, even into the very seat of reason, infecting and corrupting it, so that he judges by his fear and adjusts his behaviour accordingly. In this verse you may see the true state of the wise Stoic learnedly and plainly expressed —
"Mens immota manet; lachrymae volvuntur inanes."
["Though tears fall, the mind remains unmoved." — Virgil, Aeneid, iv. 449.]
The Peripatetic sage does not exempt himself altogether from disturbances of mind, but he moderates them.

title: The ceremony of the interview of princes
paragraphs: There is no subject so trivial that it does not deserve a place in this rhapsody. By our common rule of civility, it would be a marked insult to an equal, and much more to a superior, to fail to be at home when he has told you he will come to visit. Queen Margaret of Navarre adds, further, that it would be a rudeness in a gentleman to go out, as we so often do, to meet a man who is coming to see him, however high his condition may be; that it is more respectful and more civil to stay at home to receive him, if only to avoid missing him on the road, and that it is enough to receive him at the door and to attend on him there. For my part, anxious as I am to reduce the ceremonies of my house, I very often forget both these vain offices. If by chance someone is offended at this, I cannot help it; better to offend him once than to offend myself every day, for it would be a perpetual slavery. To what end do we avoid the servile attendance of courts, if we bring the same trouble back into our own private houses? It is also a common rule at all assemblies that the lesser sort should be on the place first, since it is more fitting to the better sort to make others wait and expect them.

Even so, at the interview between Pope Clement and King Francis at Marseilles, the king, after he had arranged everything necessary for his reception and entertainment, withdrew from the town and gave the pope two or three days' respite for his entry and to refresh himself before he came to him. And in like manner, at the meeting between the pope and the emperor at Bologna, the emperor gave the pope the chance to come there first and arrived himself after. The reason was this: that at all such meetings between princes, the greater should be first at the appointed place — especially when this is on the other's territory — implying a kind of deference to the other, since it seems proper for the lesser to seek out and present himself to the greater, and not the greater to him.

Not every country only, but every city and every society has its own particular forms of civility. There was care enough taken in my education, and I have lived in good company enough to know the formalities of our own nation, and am able to give lessons in them. I like to follow them, but not so slavishly as to enslave my whole life to ceremonies — some of them so troublesome that, provided a man omits them out of discretion and not for want of breeding, the omission will be every bit as graceful. I have seen people made rude by being over-civil and tiresome in their courtesy.

Still, these excesses aside, the knowledge of courtesy and good manners is a very necessary study. It is, like grace and beauty, what creates liking and an inclination to love one another at first sight, and at the very beginning of an acquaintance; and, consequently, it is what first opens the door and lets us in to instruct ourselves by the example of others, and to give examples ourselves, if we have any worth noticing and sharing.

title: That men are justly punished for being obstinate in the defence of a fort that is not in reason to be defended
paragraphs: Valour has its bounds as well as the other virtues, which, once crossed, the next step is into the territory of vice. So that, having too large a share of this heroic virtue, unless a man knows its limits very precisely (and on the borderline they are very hard to make out), he may easily, without realising it, run into temerity, obstinacy, and folly. From this it is that we have derived the custom, in times of war, of punishing even with death those who stubbornly defend a place that, by the rules of war, is not tenable; otherwise men would be so emboldened by the hope of impunity that not a henroost but would resist and try to hold up an army.

The Constable Monsieur de Montmorency, having at the siege of Pavia been ordered to cross the Ticino and take up his quarters in the Faubourg St Antonio, was held up by a tower at the end of the bridge so stubborn as to endure a battery; for which he hanged every man he found inside. And again, accompanying the Dauphin in his expedition over the Alps, and taking the castle of Villano by assault, where all inside had been put to the sword by the fury of the soldiers, the governor and his ensign alone excepted, he had these two trussed up too for the same reason. So also did Captain Martin du Bellay, then governor of Turin, with the governor of San Buono, in that same country, all of whose people had been cut to pieces at the taking of the place.

But since the strength or weakness of a fortress is always measured against the forces attacking it — a man might reasonably enough despise two culverins but would be a madman to face a battery of thirty cannon — and since the greatness of the prince commanding the field, his reputation, and the respect owed him are also weighed in, there is a danger that the scales tip too far in that direction. It may happen that a man becomes so impressed with himself and his power that, thinking it unreasonable for any place to dare to shut its gates against him, he puts everything to the sword wherever he meets resistance, as long as his fortune holds. So in the fierce and arrogant forms of summoning towns and declaring war, savouring of barbarian pride and insolence, that are still in use among the eastern princes — and that their successors to this day retain and practise. And in that part of the world where the Portuguese subdued the Indians, they found some states where it was a universal and inviolable law that any enemy overcome by the king in person, or by his lieutenant, was excluded from any terms at all.
So above all, of both ransom and mercy, a man should take care, if he can, of falling into the hands of a judge who is an enemy and victorious.

title: Of the punishment of cowardice
paragraphs: I once heard tell of a prince, and a great captain, who, when at his table the proceedings against Monsieur de Vervins were related to him — Vervins had been sentenced to death for surrendering Boulogne to the English — openly maintained that a soldier cannot justly be put to death for lack of courage. And, in truth, there is reason to make a great distinction between faults that merely proceed from weakness and those that are clearly the effects of treachery and malice. In the latter, we act against the rules of reason that nature has imprinted in us; whereas, in the former, it seems we might appeal to the same nature, which left us in such a state of imperfection and weakness of courage, in our own defence. So that many have thought we ought to be answerable only for what we commit against our conscience; and it is partly on this rule that those base their opinion who disapprove of capital or bloody punishments for heretics and unbelievers, and those also who hold that a judge is not accountable for having failed in his administration through mere ignorance.

But as to cowardice, it is certain that the most usual way of punishing it is by public disgrace; and the practice is supposed to have been first brought into use by the legislator Charondas. Before his time the laws of Greece punished those who fled in battle with death; he ordained that they should only, for three days, be exposed in the public square in women's clothes, hoping still to get some service from them by waking up their courage through this open shame:
"Suffundere malis hominis sanguinem, quam effundere."
["Rather to bring the blood into a man's cheek than to let it out of his body." — Tertullian, Apologetics.]

It also appears that the Roman laws once punished those with death who had run away; for Ammianus Marcellinus says that the Emperor Julian commanded ten of his soldiers, who had turned their backs in an encounter against the Parthians, to be first degraded, and afterwards put to death, in accordance, he says, with the ancient laws. And yet elsewhere, for the same kind of offence, he only condemned others to remain among the prisoners under the baggage ensign. The harsh punishment that the people of Rome inflicted on those who fled from the battle of Cannae, and on those who ran away with Cnaeus Fulvius at his defeat, did not extend to death. And yet I think there is a danger that disgrace may make such offenders desperate, and turn them not merely into half-hearted friends but into actual enemies.

Of recent memory, the Seigneur de Franget, lieutenant to the Maréchal de Châtillon's company, having by the Maréchal de Chabannes been put in charge of Fuenterrabia in place of Monsieur de Lude, and having surrendered it to the Spaniards, was for this condemned to be stripped of all nobility, and both he and his descendants declared base, taxable, and forever incapable of bearing arms — a severe sentence afterwards duly executed at Lyon. And since, all the gentlemen who were in Guise when the Count of Nassau entered it underwent the same punishment, as several others have done since for the like offence. Nevertheless, in a case of such manifest ignorance or cowardice as exceeds all ordinary example, it is only reasonable to take it as sufficient proof of treachery and malice, and to punish accordingly.

title: A proceeding of some ambassadors
paragraphs: I make it a habit in my travels to learn something from the information of those with whom I talk (which is the best school of all), and to put my companions on the subjects they are best able to speak on —
"Basti al nocchiero ragionar de' venti, Al bifolco dei tori; et le sue piaghe Conti'l guerrier; conti'l pastor gli armenti."
["Let the sailor be content to talk of the winds; the cowherd of his oxen; the soldier of his wounds; the shepherd of his flocks." — An Italian rendering of Propertius, ii. 1, 43.]

For it often happens, on the contrary, that everyone would rather hold forth on someone else's province than on his own, thinking it so much extra reputation acquired — witness the jeer Archidamus put upon Periander, that "he had given up the glory of being an excellent physician for the reputation of a very bad poet." And just observe how lavish and full Caesar is when he wants to make us understand his inventions for building bridges and contriving engines of war, and how succinct and reserved by comparison when he speaks of the offices of his profession, his own valour, and military conduct. His deeds prove him a great captain well enough, and he knew this; but he also wanted to be thought an excellent engineer — a quality somewhat outside the field, and not one we should look for in him. The elder Dionysius was a very great captain, as his fortune required; but he took a great deal of trouble to gain a private reputation as a poet, and yet he was never cut out for one. A man of the legal profession, brought not long ago to see a study furnished with all sorts of books, on his own subject and on every other, took no interest at all in any of them, but fell rather rudely and magisterially to comment on a barricade set across the spiral staircase in front of the door of the study — a thing a hundred captains and common soldiers see every day without noticing or finding fault with.
"Optat ephippia bos piger, optat arare caballus."
["The lazy ox wants a saddle and bridle; the horse wants to plough." — Horace, Epistles, i. 14, 43.]

By this kind of behaviour a man will never improve himself, nor arrive at any perfection in anything. He must make it his business always to put the architect, the painter, the sculptor, every kind of mechanical craftsman, upon discoursing on his own particular subject.

To the same purpose, in reading histories — which are everyone's subject — I am in the habit of considering what kind of men the authors are. If they are persons who profess nothing but pure letters, I principally take from them style and language; if physicians, I am the more inclined to credit what they report of the temperature of the air, of the health and complexions of princes, of wounds and diseases; if lawyers, I look to them for the controversies of rights and wrongs, the establishment of laws and civil government, and the like; if divines, the affairs of the Church, ecclesiastical censures, marriages, and dispensations; if courtiers, manners and ceremonies; if soldiers, the things that properly belong to their trade and, principally, the accounts of the actions and enterprises in which they were personally involved; if ambassadors, I look at negotiations, intelligences, and practices, and the manner in which these are conducted.

Which is why (something I would have lightly passed over in another writer) I lingered over and carefully considered one passage in the history written by Monsieur de Langey, a man of very great judgment in matters of that kind. After giving an account of the fine oration Charles V had made in the Consistory at Rome, in the presence of the Bishop of Macon and Monsieur du Velly, our ambassadors there, in which he had mixed in several injurious expressions to the dishonour of our nation — and, among the rest, "that if his captains and soldiers were not men of another stamp of fidelity, resolution, and skill in arms than those of the king, he would put a rope round his neck and immediately go to him to beg for mercy" (and the emperor seems really to have held this, or only a very slightly better, opinion of our military men, for he afterwards, twice or three times in his life, said the very same thing); as also, that he challenged the king to fight him in his shirt, with rapier and dagger, in a boat. The said Sieur de Langey, going on with his history, adds that the said ambassadors, sending a dispatch to the king on these matters, concealed the greater part, and in particular the last two passages. At which I could not but wonder, that it should be in an ambassador's power to suppress anything he ought to convey to his master, especially something of such importance as this, coming from the mouth of such a person and spoken in so great an assembly. And I should rather have thought it the servant's duty faithfully to lay the whole matter before him as it passed, so that the liberty of selecting, arranging, judging, and concluding should remain with him. For to conceal or disguise the truth out of fear that he may take it otherwise than he ought, and out of fear it may prompt him to some extreme resolution — and in the meantime to leave him in the dark about his own affairs — seems to me to belong rather to the man who is to give the law than to the one who is only to receive it; to the one in supreme command, and not to one who ought to regard himself as inferior, not only in authority but also in prudence and good counsel. I, for my part, would not be served so even in my own small affairs.

We so willingly slip the collar of command on any pretext, and are so ready to usurp dominion, every one of us so naturally aspires to liberty and power, that no advantage a superior gets from the wit or valour of those he employs ought to be as dear to him as a straightforward and sincere obedience. To obey by reason of one's own understanding rather than out of subjection is to corrupt the office of command. So it was that Publius Crassus, the man whom the Romans reckoned five times happy, when he was consul in Asia sent for a Greek engineer to bring him the larger of two ships' masts he had noticed at Athens, for use in some battery engine he meant to make. The engineer, presuming on his own skill and sufficiency in such matters, thought fit to do otherwise than directed, and brought the smaller one, which, by the rules of his art, was really more proper for the use in hand. But Crassus, though he listened to his reasons very patiently, would not, however well-grounded they were, take them as current pay, but had him soundly whipped for his pains, valuing the interest of discipline far more than the interest of the work in hand.

We may, on the other hand, consider that this kind of strict and implicit obedience is owed only to positive and limited commands. The employment of ambassadors is never so confined; much in the management of their affairs is referred entirely to their own absolute discretion. They do not simply execute, but also, by their own judgment and wisdom, shape and form their master's wishes. I have known, in my time, men in command who were taken to task for having followed the express words of the king's letters rather than the necessity of the matters they had in hand. Men of understanding still, to this day, find fault with the custom of the kings of Persia, who gave their lieutenants and agents so short a rein that, at the least difficulty arising, they had to refer back to a further order. This delay, given the great extent of their dominion, has often been seriously prejudicial to their affairs. And Crassus, writing to a man whose profession it was to know about such things, and pre-acquainting him with the use to which the mast was to be put — did he not seem to be consulting his advice, and in a way inviting him to bring his better judgment to bear?

title: Of fear
paragraphs: "Obstupui, steteruntque comae et vox faucibus haesit."
["I was amazed; my hair stood on end, and my voice stuck in my throat." — Virgil, Aeneid, ii. 774.]

I am not naturalist enough (as they call it) to make out by what secret springs fear has its motion in us; but, that aside, it is a strange passion, and one that the physicians say there is no other that more quickly dethrones our judgment from its proper seat. So true is this that I myself have seen many people become frantic with fear, and even in those of the steadiest temper it is certain that during the fit it produces a terrible bewilderment and confusion. I leave aside the common run of people, to whom it represents one moment their great-grandfathers risen from their graves in their shrouds, and another moment werewolves, nightmares, and chimeras. But even among soldiers — a sort of men over whom fear, of all others, ought to have the least power — how often has it turned flocks of sheep into armed squadrons, reeds and bulrushes into pikes and lances, friends into enemies, and the white cross of France into the red cross of Spain! When Monsieur de Bourbon took Rome, an ensign on guard at Borgo San Pietro was seized with such fright at the first alarm that he threw himself out at a breach with his colours on his shoulder and ran straight toward the enemy, thinking he had retreated towards the inner defences of the city; and only with great trouble, when he saw Monsieur de Bourbon's men, who took it for a sally upon them, drawing up to receive him, did he at last come to himself and realise his mistake. Then facing about, he retreated at top speed back through the same breach by which he had come out, but only after he had first blindly advanced more than three hundred paces into the open field. It did not turn out so well with Captain Giulio's ensign at the time when St Paul was taken from us by the Count of Bures and Monsieur de Reu, for he, so amazed with fear that he flung himself, colours and all, out of a port-hole, was immediately cut to pieces by the enemy. And in the same siege there was a very memorable fear that so seized, contracted, and froze up the heart of a gentleman that he sank down, stone-dead, in the breach, without any manner of wound or hurt at all. The like madness sometimes pushes on a whole multitude: for in one of the encounters Germanicus had with the Germans, two great parties were so seized with fear that they ran two opposite ways, the one to the very place from which the other had fled. Sometimes fear adds wings to the heels, as in the first two cases; sometimes it nails them to the ground and fetters them from moving, as we read of the Emperor Theophilus, who in a battle he lost against the Agarenes was so astonished and stupefied that he had no power to fly —
"Adeo pavor etiam auxilia formidat"
["So much does fear dread even the means of safety." — Quintus Curtius, ii. 11.]

— until Manuel, one of the principal commanders of his army, having jogged and shaken him to bring him out of his trance, said to him: "Sir, if you will not follow me, I will kill you, for it is better that you should lose your life than, by being taken, lose your empire." But fear shows its utmost power when it drives us into a valiant despair, having first stripped us of all sense of duty and honour. In the first pitched battle the Romans lost against Hannibal, under the consul Sempronius, a body of ten thousand foot that had taken fright, seeing no other escape for their cowardice, threw themselves headlong on the great battalion of the enemy, and with marvellous force and fury charged through and through it, routing it with a very great slaughter of the Carthaginians — buying themselves an inglorious flight at the same price they might have gained a glorious victory.

The thing in the world I am most afraid of is fear, a passion whose trouble exceeds any other accident at all. What grief could be greater or more just than that of Pompey's friends, who, on his ship, were spectators of that horrible murder? And yet, so it was, that the fear of the Egyptian vessels they saw bearing down to board them filled them with such alarm that it is observed they thought of nothing but urging the sailors to make haste, and by force of oars to get away — until, having reached Tyre and being delivered from fear, they had leisure to turn their thoughts to the loss of their captain and to give vent to the tears and lamentations that the other, more powerful, passion had until then held in check.
"Tum pavor sapientiam omnem mihi ex animo expectorat."
["Then fear drove all the wisdom out of my mind." — Ennius, quoted by Cicero, Tusculan Disputations, iv. 8.]

Men who have been roughly handled in some skirmish, all wounded and bloody as they are, may be brought up again the next day to charge; but those who have once felt a good sound fear of the enemy will not be made to so much as look him in the face afterwards. Men who are in immediate fear of losing their estates, of banishment, or of slavery, live in perpetual anguish and lose all appetite and rest; whereas those who are actually poor, slaves, or exiled often live as merrily as anyone else. And the many people who, unable to bear the perpetual alarms of fear, have hanged themselves, drowned themselves, or thrown themselves to pieces, are enough to convince us that fear is more importunate and unbearable than death itself.

The Greeks recognised another kind of fear, distinct from any we have spoken of, which surprises us with no visible cause, by an impulse from heaven, so that whole nations and whole armies have been struck with it. Such was the one that fell with extraordinary devastation on Carthage: nothing was to be heard but terrified voices and outcries; the inhabitants were seen rushing out of their houses as if to an alarm, and falling on one another, wounding and killing one another as if they had been enemies come to surprise the city. Everything was in confusion and fury, until at last with prayers and sacrifices they had appeased their gods. These are what they call panic terrors.

title: That men are not to judge of our happiness till after death
paragraphs: [Charron has borrowed unusually freely from this and the next chapter. See Nodier, Questions, p. 206.]
"Scilicet ultima semper Exspectanda dies homini est; dicique beatus Ante obitum nemo supremaque funera debet."
["We should all look forward to our last day; no one can be called happy till he is dead and buried." — Ovid, Metamorphoses, iii. 135.]

Even children know the story of King Croesus on this point. Taken prisoner by Cyrus and condemned by him to die, on his way to execution he cried out, "O Solon, Solon!" When this was reported to Cyrus, who sent to ask what it meant, Croesus explained that he was now finding, to his cost, how true the lesson Solon had once given him had been — namely, "that, however fortune may smile upon them, men can never be called happy until they have been seen to pass over the last day of their lives," because of the uncertainty and mutability of human things, which on the smallest and most trivial occasions are liable to be entirely changed into the contrary condition. And so it was that Agesilaus answered someone saying what a happy young man the King of Persia was, to come so young to so mighty a kingdom: "Yes," he said, "but neither was Priam unhappy at his years." In a short time, kings of Macedon, successors of that great Alexander, became carpenters and scribes at Rome; a tyrant of Sicily a schoolmaster at Corinth; a conqueror of half the world and general of so many armies, a wretched suppliant to the rascally officers of a king of Egypt — so much did the prolongation of five or six months of life cost the great Pompey. And in our fathers' days, Ludovico Sforza, the tenth Duke of Milan, under whom all Italy had so long bowed, was seen to die a wretched prisoner at Loches, but not until he had lived ten years in captivity, which was the worst part of his fortune. The fairest of all queens, widow to the greatest king in Europe — did she not come to die at the hand of an executioner? Unworthy and barbarous cruelty. And a thousand other examples there are of the same kind. It seems that, just as storms and tempests have a malice against the proud and overtowering heights of our lofty buildings, there are also spirits above that are envious of the greatnesses here below:
"Usque adeo res humanas vis abdita quaedam Obterit, et pulchros fasces, saevasque secures Proculcare, ac ludibrio sibi habere videtur."
["So true it is that some hidden power crushes human affairs, and seems to trample the glittering rods and the cruel axes underfoot and to make sport of them." — Lucretius, v. 1231.]

And it would seem, too, that Fortune sometimes lies in wait to ambush the last hour of our lives, to show the power she has, in a moment, to overthrow what she had been so many years in building, and to make us cry out with Laberius:
"Nimirum hac die Una plus vixi mihi, quam vivendum fuit."
["I have lived by this one day longer than I ought to have lived." — Macrobius, ii. 7.]

And in this sense Solon's good advice may reasonably be taken. But since he was a philosopher (and with that sort of men the favours and disgraces of Fortune count for nothing in making a man happy or unhappy, and grandeurs and powers are accidents of an almost indifferent quality), I think he had something else in mind: that the very felicity of life itself, which depends on the tranquillity and contentment of a well-born spirit and on the resolution and steadiness of a well-ordered soul, ought never to be attributed to any man until he has been seen to play the last, and doubtless the hardest, act of his part. There may be disguise and dissimulation in all the rest — where these fine philosophical discourses are only put on for show, and where mishap, not touching us to the quick, gives us leisure to keep the same gravity of look. But in this last scene of death, there is no more pretending: we must speak plainly, and show what good and clean is at the bottom of the pot.
"Nam verae voces tum demum pectore ab imo Ejiciuntur; et eripitur persona, manet res."
["Then at last truth is forced from the bottom of the heart; the mask is stripped away, the man remains." — Lucretius, iii. 57.]

This is why, at this last moment, all the other actions of our life are to be tested and sifted. It is the master-day; it is the day that is judge of all the rest. "It is the day," says one of the ancients, "that must be judge of all my preceding years." To death I refer the assaying of the fruit of all my studies; then we shall see whether my discourses came only from my mouth, or from my heart. I have seen many men by their dying give a good or a bad name to their whole life. Scipio, Pompey's father-in-law, in dying well, removed the ill opinion everyone had until then conceived of him. Epaminondas, asked which of three he most esteemed, Chabrias, Iphicrates, or himself, said: "You must first see us die before that question can be answered." And indeed it would be a great wrong to weigh him without the honour and grandeur of his end.

God has ordered all things as it has pleased him. But I have, in my time, seen three of the most loathsome men I have ever known, in every kind of abominable conduct, and the most infamous to boot, who all died very orderly deaths, composed in every circumstance, even to perfection. There are brave and fortunate deaths: I have seen death cut short the progress of a prodigious advancement, in the very flowering of its rise, in a certain man, with so glorious an end that, in my opinion, his ambitious and generous designs had nothing in them so high and great as their interruption. He arrived, without completing his course, at the place his ambition aimed for, with greater glory than he could either have hoped or wished for, anticipating by his fall the name and the power he had striven for through his career. In judging another man's life, I always observe how he carried himself at his death; and the principal concern I have for my own is that I may die well — that is, patiently and at peace.

title: That to study philosophy is to learn to die
paragraphs: Cicero says "that to study philosophy is nothing but to prepare oneself to die." The reason is that study and contemplation in some sense withdraw the soul from us and employ it apart from the body — a kind of apprenticeship and resemblance of death; or else because all the wisdom and reasoning in the world finally come down to this one point: to teach us not to fear to die. To tell the truth, either our reason is mocking us, or it ought to have no other aim than our contentment, and to strive for nothing but, in sum, to make us live well and, as Holy Scripture says, at our ease. All the opinions of the world agree on this: that pleasure is our end, though we use various means to reach it. Otherwise they would all be rejected at the first move; for who would listen to anyone proposing affliction and misery as a final goal? The disputes between the philosophical sects on this point are merely verbal:
"Transcurramus solertissimas nugas"
["Let us skip over those subtle trifles." — Seneca, Ep., 117.]

— there is more in those quarrels of contention and obstinacy than is consistent with so sacred a profession; but whatever role a man takes upon himself to play, he always mixes in his own part with it.

Let the philosophers say what they will, the thing we all aim at, even in virtue, is pleasure. It amuses me to rattle in their ears this word that so nauseates them; and if it signifies some supreme pleasure and contentment, that is more owed to the help of virtue than to any other source. This pleasure, for being more cheerful, more sinewy, more robust, and more manly, is only the more seriously voluptuous, and we ought to give it the name of pleasure as the more favourable, gentle, and natural — not the lower form from which we have borrowed the word. The other and meaner pleasure, if it deserves this fair name at all, ought to have it by way of competition, not of privilege. I find it less exempt from troubles and inconveniences than virtue itself; and besides being more momentary, fluid, and frail in its enjoyment, it has its watchings, fasts, and labours, its sweat and its blood, and is afflicted besides with so many sharp and wounding passions, and so dull a satiety following on it, that it matches the severest penance. We mistake when we think these inconveniences serve only as a spur and seasoning to its sweetness (as in nature one contrary is quickened by its opposite), or say of virtue that the same difficulties overwhelm it and render it austere and inaccessible. On the contrary — much more aptly than in pleasure, those difficulties ennoble, sharpen, and heighten the perfect and divine pleasure that virtue procures for us. He renders himself unworthy of it who weighs its cost against its fruit, and neither understands the blessing nor how to use it. Those who preach to us that the quest of virtue is rocky, difficult, and painful but the enjoyment pleasant — what do they mean by that except to tell us virtue is always unpleasing? For by what human means is its enjoyment ever attained? The most perfect have had to content themselves with aspiring to it, and approaching it only, without ever possessing it. But they are mistaken: of all the pleasures we know, the very pursuit is pleasant. The attempt takes on the quality of the thing it is aimed at, for it is a good part of, and inseparable from, the effect. The happiness and blessedness that shine in virtue shine throughout all her approaches and avenues, even to the first entry and outermost limits.

Now, of all the benefits virtue confers on us, contempt of death is one of the greatest, because it is what fits human life with a soft and easy tranquillity, and gives us a pure and pleasant taste of living, without which all other pleasures would be extinguished. This is why all the rules centre and converge on this one article. And although they all likewise teach us, by common accord, to despise pain, poverty, and the other accidents human life is subject to, it is not with the same urgency — partly because those accidents are not so inevitable (the greater part of mankind pass their whole lives without ever knowing what poverty is, and some without sorrow or sickness, like Xenophilus the musician, who lived a hundred and six years in perfect and continual health); and partly because, at the worst, death can whenever we please cut short and put an end to all other inconveniences. But death itself is inevitable:
"Omnes eodem cogimur; omnium Versatur urna serius ocius Sors exitura, et nos in aeternum Exilium impositura cymbae."
["We are all bound one voyage; the lot of all, sooner or later, is to come out of the urn. All must sail away to eternal exile." — Hor., Od., ii. 3, 25.]

And consequently, if death frightens us, it is a perpetual torment for which there is no kind of consolation. There is no way by which it may not reach us. We may continually turn our heads this way and that, as in a country full of ambushes:
"Quae, quasi saxum Tantalo, semper impendet."
["Ever, like Tantalus' stone, it hangs over us." — Cicero, De Finib., i. 18.]
Our courts of justice often send condemned criminals back to be executed on the spot where the crime was committed; but on the way, take them to fine houses, lay on the best entertainment you can —
"Non Siculae dapes Dulcem elaborabunt saporem: Non avium cyatheaceae cantus Somnum reducent."
["Sicilian dainties will not tickle their palates, nor the melody of birds and harps bring back sleep." — Hor., Od., iii. 1, 18.]
Do you think they can enjoy any of it? Do you think the fatal end of their journey, constantly before their eyes, would not alter and spoil their taste for these delicacies?
"Audit iter, numeratque dies, spatioque viarum Metitur vitam; torquetur peste futura."
["He considers the route, counts the days of the journey, measures his life by the length of the road, and torments himself by thinking of the blow to come." — Claudianus, in Ruf., ii. 137.]

The end of our race is death. It is the necessary object of our aim, and if it frightens us, how is it possible to take a single step forward without a fit of fever? The remedy ordinary people use is not to think about it; but what brutish stupidity could produce so gross a blindness? They are trying to bridle the ass by the tail:
"Qui capite ipse suo instituit vestigia retro,"
["Who in his folly seeks to advance backwards." — Lucretius, iv. 474.]

No wonder he so often falls into the pit. They terrify people with the very word death, and many cross themselves as if at the name of the devil. And because making one's will refers to dying, no one can be persuaded to take up a pen for that purpose until the physician has passed sentence on him and given him over altogether; and then, between pain and terror, God knows in how fit a condition of understanding he is to do it.

The Romans, finding that this poor syllable death sounded so harshly to their ears and seemed so ominous, found a way to soften and spin it out by a circumlocution. Instead of saying "So-and-so is dead," they said "So-and-so has lived," or "So-and-so has ceased to live" — for, provided there was any mention of life in the phrase, even past life, it carried some sound of consolation. From them we borrowed our expression, "The late Monsieur So-and-so." Perhaps, as the saying goes, the words we have lived are worth our money. I was born between eleven and twelve o'clock in the forenoon on the last day of February 1533, by our reckoning, which begins the year on the 1st of January; and it is now just fifteen days since I turned thirty-nine years old, complete. I expect to live, at least, as many more. In the meantime, it would be folly to trouble myself with the thought of a thing so far off. But what? Young and old die on the same terms; no one leaves life otherwise than as if he had just entered it. And no man is so old and decrepit that, having heard of Methuselah, he does not think he has another twenty good years to come. Fool that you are! Who has guaranteed you the term of your life? You depend on physicians' tales: rather consult facts and experience. By the common course of things, you have for some time been living by extraordinary favour; you have already outlived the ordinary span. To prove it, count up your acquaintances and see how many more have died before reaching your age than have made it; and of those who ennobled their lives by their fame, just keep a tally, and I will lay you a wager you will find more who died before than after thirty-five. It is both reasonable and pious to take Jesus Christ Himself for an example: He ended His life at thirty-three. The greatest man who was no more than a man, Alexander, died also at the same age. How many ways death has to surprise us!
"Quid quisque, vitet, nunquam homini satis Cautum est in horas."
["Be as cautious as he may, no man can ever foresee the danger that may befall him at any hour." — Hor., Od., ii. 13, 13.]

To say nothing of fevers and pleurisies, who would ever have imagined that a Duke of Brittany would be crushed to death in a crowd, as that duke was at the entry of Pope Clement, my neighbour, into Lyons? Have you not seen one of our kings killed at a tilting match, and one of his ancestors die from being jostled by a hog? Aeschylus, warned of being killed by the fall of a house, took every possible precaution — and was knocked on the head by a tortoise dropped out of an eagle's talons in the air. Another man was choked by a grape-seed; an emperor was killed by the scratch of a comb while combing his hair. Aemilius Lepidus died by stumbling at his own threshold, and Aufidius by knocking against the door as he entered the council chamber. And between the very thighs of women: Cornelius Gallus the praetor; Tigillinus, captain of the watch at Rome; Ludovico, son of Guido di Gonzaga, Marquis of Mantua; and (a worse example) Speusippus, a Platonic philosopher, and one of our Popes. Poor Judge Bebius granted a postponement in a case for eight days; but in the meantime he himself was condemned by death, and his own stay of life expired. While Caius Julius the physician was anointing the eyes of a patient, death closed his own. And if I may bring in an example of my own blood: a brother of mine, Captain St. Martin, a young man of twenty-three who had already given sufficient proof of his courage, was playing a match at tennis when he received a blow from a ball a little above his right ear. As it left no sign of wound or bruise, he took no notice and did not even sit down to rest; nevertheless he died within five or six hours of an apoplexy caused by that blow.

With these frequent and ordinary examples passing every day before our eyes, how is it possible for a man to free himself from the thought of death, or to avoid fancying that it has us every moment by the throat? What does it matter, you will say, which way it comes, provided a man does not torment himself with the expectation? For my part, I am of this mind, and if a man could by any means avoid death — even by creeping under a calf's skin — I am one who would not be ashamed of the shift. All I aim at is to pass my time at my ease, and I take hold of whichever recreations contribute most to that, however little glorious or exemplary you may find them:
"Praetulerim . . . delirus inersque videri, Dum mea delectent mala me, vel denique fallant, Quam sapere, et ringi."
["I had rather seem mad and a sluggard, so long as my faults please me, or that I am not painfully aware of them, than be wise and snarling." — Hor., Ep., ii. 2, 126.]

But it is folly to think one can pull this off. They go, they come, they gallop and dance, and not a word of death. All very fine — but when it comes to themselves, their wives, their children, or their friends, surprising them off-guard and unprepared, what torment, what outcry, what madness and despair! Did you ever see anything so beaten down, so changed, so confounded? A man must therefore make earlier provision for it; and this brutish negligence — could it possibly lodge in the brain of any man of sense (which I think utterly impossible) — sells us its merchandise far too dearly. Were death an enemy that could be avoided, I would then advise borrowing arms even from cowardice itself; but since it cannot be avoided, and since it will catch you fleeing and playing the coward just as well as standing your ground like an honest man:
"Nempe et fugacem persequitur virum, Nec parcit imbellis juventae Poplitibus timidoque tergo."
["He pursues the fleeing coward, nor spares the hamstrings of the unwarlike youth who turns his back." — Hor., Ep., iii. 2, 14.]
And since no armour is proof against him:
"Ille licet ferro cautus, se condat et aere, Mors tamen inclusum protrahet inde caput"
["Let him hide beneath iron or brass in his fear, death will pull his head out of his armour." — Propertius, iii. 18.]

— let us learn to stand our ground bravely and fight him. And to begin to deprive him of the greatest advantage he has over us, let us take a way directly opposite to the common course. Let us disarm him of his novelty and strangeness, let us converse and be familiar with him, and have nothing so constantly in our thoughts as death. On every occasion let us picture him to our imagination in every shape: at the stumbling of a horse, at the falling of a tile, at the smallest prick of a pin, let us immediately consider and say to ourselves, "Well, and what if it had been death itself?" — and from there fortify and encourage ourselves. In the midst of our jollity and feasting, let us always set the remembrance of our frail condition before our eyes, never allowing ourselves to be so carried away by our pleasures that we have no intervals for reflecting on, and considering, how many ways this very jollity tends towards death, and with how many dangers it is shadowed. The Egyptians used to do this: at the height of their feasting and mirth, they would have a dried human skeleton brought into the room as a memento to their guests:
"Omnem crede diem tibi diluxisse supremum Grata superveniet, quae non sperabitur, hora."
["Think every day, when it is over, your last; the next, as unhoped-for, will be the more welcome." — Hor., Ep., i. 4, 13.]

Where death waits for us is uncertain; let us look for him everywhere. The premeditation of death is the premeditation of liberty. He who has learned to die has unlearned to be a slave. There is nothing evil in life for him who rightly understands that the loss of life is no evil; to know how to die delivers us from all subjection and constraint. Paulus Aemilius answered the man whom the wretched King of Macedon, his prisoner, had sent to beg him not to lead him in his triumph: "Let him make that request to himself."

In truth, in all things, if nature does not help a little, it is very hard for art and effort to accomplish much to the purpose. I am not by nature melancholy, but meditative; and there is nothing I have entertained myself with more continually than imaginations of death — even in the most carefree time of my youth:
"Jucundum quum aetas florida ver ageret."
["When my flowering age rejoiced in pleasant spring." — Catullus, lxviii.]

In the company of ladies, and at games, some have perhaps thought me preoccupied with some jealousy, or the uncertainty of some hope, when in fact I was entertaining myself with the memory of someone caught up, a few days earlier, by a burning fever of which he died, returning from an entertainment like this one with his head full of idle fancies of love and merriment, as mine then was — and that, for all I knew, the same destiny might be waiting for me.
"Jam fuerit, nec post unquam revocare licebit."
["Soon the present will have gone, never to be called back." — Lucretius, iii. 928.]

Yet such a thought did not wrinkle my forehead any more than another did. It is impossible not to feel a sting in such imaginings at first; but with often turning and returning them in one's mind, they finally become so familiar as to be no trouble at all. Otherwise, for my part, I should be in perpetual fright and frenzy; for no man was ever more distrustful of his life than I, nor more uncertain as to its duration. Neither the health I have so far enjoyed — strong and vigorous, and very seldom interrupted — prolongs my expectations, nor does sickness shorten them. Every minute, it seems to me, I am escaping; and the thought constantly runs through my mind that what may be done tomorrow may be done today. Hazards and dangers do, in truth, little or nothing to hasten our end; and if we consider how many thousands more hang over our heads besides the accident that immediately threatens us, we shall find that the healthy and the sick, those at sea and those by the fire, those engaged in battle and those sitting idle at home, are all equally near to it.
"Nemo altero fragilior est; nemo in crastinum sui certior."
["No man is more fragile than another; no man more certain than another of tomorrow." — Seneca, Ep., 91.]
For whatever I have to do before I die, the longest leisure would seem too short, even if it were only an hour's business I had on hand.

A friend of mine, the other day, leafing through my tablets, found there a note of something I wanted done after my death; I told him, and it was the truth, that though I was no more than a league from home, well and merry, when the thing came into my head I had hurried to write it down there, because I was not certain to live till I came home. As a man eternally brooding over his own thoughts, and confining them to his own particular concerns, I am at all hours as well prepared as I am ever likely to be; and death, whenever he comes, can bring nothing along with him that I have not been expecting for a long time. We should always, as nearly as we can, be booted and spurred and ready to go; and above all things, at that hour, take care to have no business with anyone but ourselves:
"Quid brevi fortes jaculamur avo Multa?"
["Why for so brief a life tease ourselves with so many projects?" — Hor., Od., ii. 16, 17.]

For we shall there find work enough to do, without any need of addition. One man complains, more than of death, that he is by it prevented from a glorious victory; another, that he must die before he has married off his daughter or educated his children; a third regrets only the loss of his wife's company; a fourth, the conversation of his son, as the chief comfort and concern of his life. For my part, I am — thanks be to God — at this moment in such a state that I am ready to move on whenever it shall please Him, without regret for anything whatsoever. I disengage myself completely from all worldly relations; my leave is soon taken of all but myself. Never did anyone prepare to say goodbye to the world more absolutely and unreservedly, or shake hands more completely with all interest in it, than I expect to do. The deadest deaths are the best:
"'Miser, O miser,' aiunt, 'omnia ademit Una dies infesta mihi tot praemia vitae.'"
["'Wretch that I am,' they cry, 'one fatal day has deprived me of all the joys of life.'" — Lucretius, iii. 911.]
And the builder,
"Manuet," says he, "opera interrupta, minaeque Murorum ingentes."
["The works remain unfinished, the tall pinnacles of the walls unmade." — Aeneid, iv. 88.]
A man should plan nothing that will need so much time to finish — or at least, with no such passionate desire to see it through to perfection. We are born to action:
"Quum moriar, medium solvar et inter opus."
["When I shall die, let me be in the midst of what I had designed." — Ovid, Amor., ii. 10, 36.]

I would always have a man busy, and, as far as in him lies, extending and spinning out the offices of life; and then let death take me planting my cabbages, indifferent to him and still less troubled that my garden is not finished. I once saw a man die who, at his last gasp, complained of nothing so much as that destiny was about to cut the thread of a chronicle he was then compiling, and he was only as far as the fifteenth or sixteenth of our kings:
"Illud in his rebus non addunt: nec tibi earum jam desiderium rerum super insidet una."
["They do not add this: that dying, the desire for those things no longer hangs about us." — Lucretius, iii. 913.]

We must disengage ourselves from these common and hurtful humours. It was for this reason that men first placed cemeteries adjoining the churches, and in the most frequented parts of the city — to accustom, says Lycurgus, the common people, women, and children, so they should not be startled at the sight of a corpse; and that the continual sight of bones, graves, and funeral rites should keep us mindful of our frail condition:
"Quin etiam exhilarare viris convivia caede Mos olim, et miscere epulis spectacula dira Certantum ferro, saepe et super ipsa cadentum Pocula, respersis non parco sanguine mensis."

["It was formerly the custom to enliven banquets with slaughter, and to combine with the meal the dire spectacle of men contending with the sword — the dying often falling upon the cups and covering the tables with blood." — Silius Italicus, xi. 51.]

And as the Egyptians, after their feasts, used to present the company with a great image of death, while one cried out to them, "Drink and be merry, for such you shall be when you are dead," so it is my custom to have death not only in my imagination but continually in my mouth. There is nothing I am so curious to inform myself of as the manner of men's deaths — their words, their looks, their bearing; nor any passages in history I am so intent upon. It is plain enough, by my crowding in examples of this kind, that I have a particular fancy for the subject. If I were a writer of books, I would compile a register, with commentary, of the various deaths of men: he who would teach men to die would at the same time teach them to live. Dicaearchus made one and gave it that title, but designed it for a different and less profitable end.

Perhaps someone will object that the pain and terror of dying so infinitely exceed all imagination, that the best fencer will be quite out of his play when it comes to the push. Let them say what they will: to premeditate is no doubt a very great advantage; and besides, is it nothing to go so far, at least, without disturbance or alteration? Moreover, Nature herself helps and encourages us. If death is sudden and violent, we have no leisure to fear it; if otherwise, I notice that, as I sink further into my illness, I naturally fall into a certain loathing and disdain of life. I find I have much more trouble digesting the thought of dying when I am in good health than when I am languishing of a fever; and the less hold I have on the comforts of life — beginning to lose the use and pleasure of them — the less terror I feel at death. This makes me hope that the further I get from the first state, and the nearer I come to the second, the more easily I shall exchange the one for the other. And just as I have found in other matters, as Caesar says, that things often appear greater to us at a distance than close at hand, I have found that, being well, I have held maladies in much greater horror than when really afflicted with them. The vigour I am in now, the cheerfulness and delight in which I now live, make the contrary state appear in so great a disproportion to my present condition that, by imagination, I magnify those inconveniences by half, and apprehend them to be much more troublesome than I actually find them to be when they lie heaviest upon me. I hope to find death the same.

Let us only observe, in the ordinary changes and declinations we daily undergo, how nature deprives us of the awareness and sense of our bodily decay. What remains to an old man of the vigour of his youth, of his better days?
"Heu! senibus vitae portio quanta manet."
["Alas, what a small portion of life remains to old men!" — Maximian, or Pseudo-Gallus, i. 16.]

Caesar, to an old, weather-beaten soldier of his guard who came to ask leave to kill himself, taking notice of his withered body and decrepit movements, answered pleasantly, "You fancy, then, that you are still alive?" Should a man fall suddenly into this condition, I do not think human nature capable of enduring such a change; but nature, leading us by the hand at an easy and almost imperceptible pace, step by step conducts us into that miserable state and so makes it familiar, that we feel no shock when our youth dies in us, though it is really a harder death than the final dissolution of a languishing body — than the death of old age. For the fall is not so great from an uneasy being to none at all as it is from a sprightly and flourishing being to one that is troublesome and painful. The body, bent and bowed, has less force to support a burden; and it is the same with the soul. We must therefore raise her up firm and erect against the power of this adversary. For so long as she stands in fear of him, she can never be at rest; but if she can once assure herself, she may boast — a thing almost surpassing the human condition — that anxiety, disquiet, fear, or any other disturbance is incapable of inhabiting or having any place in her:
"Non vulnus instants Tyranni Mentha cadi solida, neque Auster Dux inquieti turbidus Adriae, Nec fulminantis magna Jovis manus."

["Not the threatening look of a tyrant shakes her well-settled mind, nor the turbulent Auster, prince of the stormy Adriatic, nor the great hand of thundering Jove — such a temper they cannot move." — Hor., Od., iii. 3, 3.]

She has then become sovereign over all her lusts and passions, mistress of necessity, of shame, of poverty, and of all the other injuries of fortune. Let us, then, as many as can, gain this advantage; it is the true and sovereign liberty here on earth, that fortifies us to defy violence and injustice, and to despise prisons and chains:
"In manicis et Compedibus saevo te sub custode tenebo. Ipse Deus, simul atque volam, me solvet. Opinor, Hoc sentit; moriar; mors ultima linea rerum est."
["I will keep you in fetters and chains, under a savage keeper. — A god, when I ask Him, will set me free. This god, I think, is death. Death is the end of all things." — Hor., Ep., i. 16, 76.]

Our very religion has no surer human foundation than the contempt of life. Not only does reason invite us to it — for why should we fear to lose a thing which, being lost, cannot be lamented? — but, also, since we are threatened by so many sorts of death, is it not infinitely worse to fear them all eternally than to undergo one of them once? And what does it matter when it comes, since it is inevitable? To the man who told Socrates, "The thirty tyrants have sentenced you to death," he replied, "And nature them." What a ridiculous thing it is to trouble ourselves about taking the one step that delivers us from all trouble! As our birth brought us the birth of all things, so our death includes the death of all things. Therefore to lament that we shall not be alive a hundred years hence is the same folly as to be sorry we were not alive a hundred years ago. Death is the beginning of another life. So did we weep, and so much did it cost us, to enter into this one, and so did we put off our former veil in entering it. Nothing can be a grievance that happens only once. Is it reasonable to be afraid for so long of a thing that will be dispatched so quickly? Long life and short are by death made all one; for there is no long, nor short, for things that are no more. Aristotle tells us there are certain little creatures on the banks of the river Hypanis that live no more than a day: those which die at eight in the morning die young, and those that die at five in the evening die in their decrepitude. Which of us would not laugh to see this moment of existence treated as a matter of weal or woe? The most and the least of ours, in comparison with eternity, or even with the duration of mountains, rivers, stars, trees, and some animals, is no less ridiculous.

But nature compels us to it. "Go out of this world," she says, "as you entered it. The same passage you made from death to life, without passion or fear — make the same again, in the same way, from life to death. Your death is part of the order of the universe; it is part of the life of the world.
"Inter se mortales mutua vivunt ................................ Et, quasi cursores, vitai lampada tradunt."
["Mortals, amongst themselves, live by turns, and, like the runners in the games, give up the lamp, when they have won the race, to the next comer." — Lucretius, ii. 75, 78.]

"Shall I alter this beautiful arrangement of things for you? It is the condition of your creation. Death is a part of you, and while you try to evade it, you evade yourselves. This very being of yours that you now enjoy is equally divided between life and death. The day of your birth is one day's advance towards the grave:
"Prima, qux vitam dedit, hora carpsit."
["The first hour that gave us life took away also an hour of it." — Seneca, Her. Fur., 3 Chor. 874.]
"Nascentes morimur, finisque ab origine pendet."
["As we are born we die, and the end commences with the beginning." — Manilius, Ast., iv. 16.]

"All the time you live, you steal from life and live at the expense of life itself. The perpetual work of your life is but to lay the foundation of death. You are in death while you are in life, because you still are after death, when you are no longer alive — or, if you prefer it the other way, you are dead after life, but dying all the while you live; and death handles the dying much more roughly than the dead, and more sensibly and essentially. If you have made profit of life, you have had enough of it; go your way satisfied.
"Cur non ut plenus vita; conviva recedis?"
["Why not depart from life as a sated guest from a feast?" — Lucretius, iii. 951.]
"If you have not known how to make the best use of it, if it was no good to you, what need have you to care about losing it? Why would you want to keep it longer?
"'Cur amplius addere quaeris, Rursum quod pereat male, et ingratum occidat omne?'
["Why seek to add longer life, merely to renew ill-spent time and be again tormented?" — Lucretius, iii. 914.]

"Life in itself is neither good nor evil; it is the scene of good or evil as you make it.' And if you have lived a day, you have seen all: one day is equal and like all other days. There is no other light, no other shade; this very sun, this moon, these very stars, this very order and arrangement of things, is the same your ancestors enjoyed, and shall also entertain your posterity:
"'Non alium videre patres, aliumve nepotes Aspicient.'
["Your grandsires saw no other thing; nor will your posterity." — Manilius, i. 529.]

"And, come the worst that can come, the distribution and variety of all the acts of my comedy are played out in a year. If you have observed the revolution of my four seasons, they contain the infancy, the youth, the manhood, and the old age of the world. The year has played its part, and knows no other art but to begin again. It will always be the same thing:
"'Versamur ibidem, atque insumus usque.'
["We are turning in the same circle, ever confined within it." — Lucretius, iii. 1093.]
"'Atque in se sua per vestigia volvitur annus.'
["The year is ever turning around in the same footsteps." — Virgil, Georg., ii. 402.]
"I am not prepared to create for you any new diversions:
"'Nam tibi prxterea quod machiner, inveniamque Quod placeat, nihil est; eadem sunt omnia semper.'
["I can devise, nor find, anything else to please you: it is the same thing over and over again." — Lucretius, iii. 957.]

"Give place to others, as others have given place to you. Equality is the soul of equity. Who can complain of being included in the same fate that all are involved in? Besides, live as long as you can — you shall by that not shorten by a moment the span you are to be dead; it is all to no purpose. You shall be as long in the condition you so much fear as if you had died at the breast:
"'Licet quot vis vivendo vincere secla, Mors aeterna tamen nihilominus illa manebit.'
["Live triumphing over as many ages as you will, death will still remain eternal." — Lucretius, iii. 1103.]
"And yet I will place you in such a condition that you shall have no reason to be displeased.
"'In vera nescis nullum fore morte alium te, Qui possit vivus tibi to lugere peremptum, Stansque jacentem.'
["Do you not know that, when dead, there can be no other living self to lament you dead, standing over your grave." — Idem., ibid., 898.]
"Nor will you so much as wish for the life you are now so concerned about:
"'Nec sibi enim quisquam tum se vitamque requirit. .................................................. "'Nec desiderium nostri nos afficit ullum.'
"Death is less to be feared than nothing, if there could be anything less than nothing.
"'Multo . . . mortem minus ad nos esse putandium, Si minus esse potest, quam quod nihil esse videmus.'

"Nor can it concern you, in any way, whether you are living or dead: living, because you are still in being; dead, because you are no more. Moreover, no one dies before his hour: the time you leave behind was no more yours than the time that lapsed and went by before you came into the world, nor does it any more concern you.
"'Respice enim, quam nil ad nos anteacta vetustas Temporis aeterni fuerit.'
["Consider how the old age of times past is as nothing to us." — Lucretius, iii. 985.]

Wherever your life ends, it is all there. The use of living lies not in the length of days, but in the use of time; a man may have lived long and yet lived little. Make use of time while it is present with you. It depends on your will, and not on the number of days, to have a sufficient length of life. Is it possible you imagine you will never arrive at the place towards which you are continually going? And yet there is no journey but has its end. And if company will make it more pleasant or easier for you, does not all the world go the very same way?
"'Omnia te, vita perfuncta, sequentur.'
["All things, then, life over, must follow you." — Lucretius, iii. 981.]

"Does not all the world dance the same dance you do? Is there anything that does not grow old, as well as you? A thousand men, a thousand animals, a thousand other creatures die the same moment you die:
"'Nam nox nulla diem, neque noctem aurora sequuta est, Quae non audierit mistos vagitibus aegris Ploratus, mortis comites et funeris atri.'
["No night has followed day, no day has followed night, in which there have not been heard sobs and sorrowing cries, the companions of death and dark funerals." — Lucretius, v. 579.]

"To what purpose should you try to draw back, if there is no way to evade it? You have seen plenty of examples of those who were well content to die, as thereby delivered from heavy miseries; but have you ever found any who were dissatisfied with dying? It must therefore be very foolish to condemn a thing you have not experienced either in your own person or in anyone else's. Why do you complain of me and of destiny? Do we do you any wrong? Is it for you to govern us, or for us to govern you? Though, perhaps, your years are not complete, yet your life is. A man of small stature is as much a man as a giant; neither men nor their lives are measured by the yard. Chiron refused to be immortal when he was told the conditions on which he was to enjoy it, by the god of time itself and its duration, his father Saturn. Just seriously consider how much more unbearable and painful an immortal life would be to man than the life I have already given him. If you had not death, you would eternally curse me for having deprived you of it. I have mixed a little bitterness with it, so that, seeing how convenient it is, you might not too greedily and indiscreetly seek to embrace it; and so that you might be so settled in this moderation as neither to be sick of life nor to have any antipathy for dying — which I have decreed you shall do once — I have tempered both of them between pleasure and pain. It was I that taught Thales, the most eminent of your sages, that to live and to die were indifferent, which made him, very wisely, answer the man who asked him why he did not die: 'Because,' he said, 'it is indifferent.' Water, earth, air, and fire, and the other parts of this creation of mine, are no more instruments of your life than they are of your death. Why do you fear your last day? It contributes no more to your dissolution than every one of the rest. The last step is not the cause of your weariness; it only declares it. Every day travels towards death; the last only arrives at it." These are the good lessons our mother Nature teaches.

I have often wondered why it should be that in war the image of death, whether we look at it in ourselves or in others, appears, beyond comparison, less dreadful than at home in our own houses (for if it were not so, the army would be made up of doctors and whining milksops); and that, since death is the same in all places, there should nevertheless be much more steadiness in peasants and common people than in those of higher rank. I truly believe it is those terrible ceremonies and preparations we surround it with that frighten us more than the thing itself: a new, quite contrary way of living; the cries of mothers, wives, and children; the visits of stunned and grieving friends; the attendance of pale and snivelling servants; a dark room set round with burning tapers; our beds surrounded by physicians and priests — in sum, nothing but ghostliness and horror around us. We seem dead and buried already. Children are afraid even of those they know best, when disguised behind a mask; and so it is with us. The mask must be removed from things as well as from persons; once it is taken away, we shall find underneath nothing but the very same death that a mean servant or a poor chambermaid died a day or two ago, without any kind of apprehension. Happy is the death that deprives us of leisure for preparing such ceremonials.

title: Of the force of imagination
paragraphs: "Fortis imaginatio generat casum," say the schoolmen.
["A strong imagination begets the event itself." — Axiom. Scholast.]

I am one of those who feel the power of imagination most strongly. Everyone is jostled by it, but some are knocked flat by it. It makes a very piercing impression upon me, and I make it my business to dodge it, lacking the strength to resist. I could live by the help of cheerful, healthy company alone: the mere sight of another's pain materially pains me, and I often take over the sensations of another person. A perpetual cough in someone else tickles my own lungs and throat. I more unwillingly visit a sick person I love and owe duty to than one I am indifferent about. I take possession of the disease I am concerned with, and lodge it in myself. I am not at all surprised that fancy gives fevers and sometimes kills people who give it too much scope and are too willing to indulge it. Simon Thomas was a great physician of his day. I remember meeting him one day at Toulouse at the house of a rich old fellow troubled with weak lungs. Discussing the method of cure with the patient, the doctor told him that one helpful thing would be for him to give me reason to enjoy his company so much that I would come often to see him; by which means, fixing his eyes on my fresh complexion and his imagination on the sprightliness and vigour glowing in my youth, and filling all his senses with the flourishing age I was then in, his bodily state might perhaps be improved. But the doctor forgot to say that mine, at the same time, might be made worse. Gallus Vibius bent his mind so hard on finding out the essence and motions of madness that, in the end, he went out of his wits himself, and to such a degree that he could never afterwards recover his judgment, and might boast he had become a fool by too much wisdom. Some men, through fear, anticipate the hangman; and there was the man whose eyes, on being unbound to have his pardon read to him, were found stark dead upon the scaffold, by the stroke of imagination alone. We start, tremble, turn pale, and blush as we are variously moved by imagination; and lying in bed we feel our bodies stirred by its power to such a degree that we sometimes expire from it. And boiling youth, when fast asleep, grows so heated with fancy as in a dream to satisfy amorous desires:
"Ut, quasi transactis saepe omnibu rebu, profundant Fluminis ingentes, fluctus, vestemque cruentent."

Though it is no new thing to see horns grown overnight on the forehead of one who had none when he went to bed, what happened to Cippus, King of Italy, is memorable: having one day been a delighted spectator at a bullfight, and having dreamed all night that he had horns on his head, he actually, by force of imagination, caused them to grow there. Passion gave to the son of Croesus the voice that nature had denied him. And Antiochus fell into a fever, inflamed by the beauty of Stratonice too deeply imprinted in his soul. Pliny claims to have seen Lucius Cossitius, who from a woman was turned into a man on her wedding day itself. Pontanus and others report a similar metamorphosis happening in our own time in Italy. And, through the vehement desire of himself and his mother:
"Volta puer solvit, quae foemina voverat, Iphis."

I myself, passing through Vitry-le-François, saw a man whom the Bishop of Soissons had named Germain in confirmation, whom all the inhabitants of the place had known to be a girl until the age of twenty-two, called Mary. He was, at the time I was there, full of beard, old, and unmarried. He told us that by straining himself in a leap his male organs had come out; and the girls of the place have, to this day, a song warning each other not to take too great strides, for fear of being turned into men, as Mary Germain was. It is no wonder if this kind of accident happens often; for if imagination has any power in such matters, the desire is so continually and vigorously fixed on this subject that, in order not to relapse into the same thought and violence of longing, it would be better, once for all, to give these young girls the things they crave.

Some attribute the scars of King Dagobert and of St. Francis to the force of imagination. It is said that by it bodies will sometimes be moved from their places; and Celsus tells us of a priest whose soul would be carried away into such an ecstasy that his body would for a long time remain without sense or breath. St. Augustine mentions another who, on hearing any lamentable or doleful cries, would immediately fall into a swoon and be so far out of himself that it was no use calling out, bawling in his ears, pinching or burning him until he voluntarily came to. Then he would say he had heard voices as it were far off, and had felt them pinching and burning him; and, to show that this was no obstinate dissimulation in defiance of his sense of feeling, it was clear that all the while he had neither pulse nor breath.

It is very probable that visions, enchantments, and all extraordinary effects of that kind derive their credit chiefly from the power of imagination, working and making its strongest impression on common and easily-led souls, whose belief is so strangely imposed upon that they think they see what they do not see.

I am not sure whether those curious bewitchings of bridegrooms our age is so taken up with — there is hardly any other topic of talk — are not simply voluntary impressions of apprehension and fear. For I know, from experience, in the case of a particular friend of mine, a man I can vouch for as for myself, and one quite incapable of falling under any suspicion of inadequacy, and as little of being bewitched: having heard a companion of his describe a sudden frigidity that had overtaken him at an awkward moment, when he himself was afterwards engaged on the same business, the horror of the previous story so strangely possessed his imagination that he met the same fate the other had. From then on, the wretched memory of that disaster running in his mind and tyrannising over him, he kept relapsing into the same misfortune. He found some remedy, however, for this fancy by means of another fancy: by frankly confessing and declaring his weakness in advance to the woman he was with, the agitation of his soul was, in some measure, calmed; and once it was known that some such mishap was expected from him, the constraint on his faculties grew less. Afterwards, on occasions when he was in no such apprehension — his thoughts being free and his body in its natural state — he was able to have the part handled and brought to the knowledge of the other party, and so was entirely freed from that vexatious infirmity.
